hero.title: Abstract types and overriding
intro.0: A type does not have to be a plain bag of data. It can describe a shape it refuses to build itself, replace a behaviour it inherited, answer to one name for different inputs, choose how it prints, and clean up after itself at a known point. You write each of these and run it.
task.1.title: A type you cannot make
task.1.context:
Some types describe a **shape** without being a thing you can make. `Animal` says every animal can `Speak`, but there is no such thing as a plain animal - only a cat, a dog, a cow. A type like that is **abstract**: it defines what its subtypes must provide, and cannot itself be created with `new`.

An abstract method has no body - each subtype writes its own. Give `Cat` a `Speak` that returns its sound.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Cat` an `override string Speak()` that returns `"Meow"`.
task.1.goal.1: `Main` holds the cat in an `Animal` variable and prints `Speak()`, so the output is `Meow`.
task.2.title: Replace a default
task.2.context:
Sometimes a base type has a sensible **default** behaviour, and a subtype wants to **replace** it. Mark the base method `virtual` to say "this can be replaced"; mark the subtype's version `override` to replace it. Code holding the base type still calls through to whichever version the real object carries.

Here: `Pet` has a default `Sound`. Make `Parrot` override it with the parrot's own.
task.2.goal.1: Give `Parrot` an `override string Sound()` that returns `"Squawk"`.
task.2.goal.2: `Main` holds the parrot in a `Pet` variable and prints `Sound()`, so the output is `Squawk`.
task.3.title: One name, different inputs
task.3.context:
One operation can make sense with different inputs. **Overloading** lets you give two methods the same name but different parameters; the compiler picks the right one from the arguments you pass. It keeps a single clear name instead of `AddOne` and `AddTwo`.

Here: give `Counter` two `Add` methods - one takes a single number, one takes two - and return their total.
task.3.goal.0: Give `Counter` an `int Add(int a)` that returns `a`.
task.3.goal.1: Give `Counter` a second `int Add(int a, int b)` that returns `a + b`.
task.4.title: A type's own text form
task.4.context:
By default, printing an object shows its type name - not useful. **Overriding `ToString`** lets a type decide its own text form, so `Console.WriteLine(obj)` shows something meaningful. Anywhere the object is turned into text, your version is used.

Here: give `Cat` a `ToString` that returns `"Cat: "` followed by its name.
task.4.goal.0: Give `Cat` an `override string ToString()` that returns `"Cat: "` joined with its `name`.
task.4.goal.1: `Main` prints the cat with `Console.WriteLine(c)`, so a cat named `Whiskers` reads `Cat: Whiskers`.
task.5.title: Clean up at a known point
task.5.context:
Some things must be **cleaned up** when you are done - a file closed, a connection dropped - and you want that to happen at a known point, not whenever. A type that implements **`IDisposable`** has a `Dispose` method for exactly that. A `using` block calls `Dispose` for you the moment the block ends, even if something inside it fails.

Here: `Cage` prints `"open"` when built. Make its `Dispose` print `"closed"` so the `using` block cleans up deterministically.
task.5.goal.1: `Main` wraps the cage in a `using` block, so the output is `open` then `closed`.
task.6.title: What you learned
task.6.context: Five ways to make a type carry its own behaviour - the everyday tools of a type system, portable to most object languages.
task.6.summaryIntro: You gave types their own shape and behaviour, one piece at a time:
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: A type you cannot make -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: an `abstract` base defines what subtypes must provide and cannot be created on its own, so `Cat` and `Dog` fill in the `Speak` it only declares.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: Replace a default -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: a `virtual` method offers a default and an `override` replaces it, while code holding the base type still calls the real object's version.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: One name, different inputs -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: **overloading** gives two methods the same name with different parameters, so `Add(2)` and `Add(2, 3)` read naturally.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: A type's own text form -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: overriding `ToString` decides how the object prints, so `Console.WriteLine(obj)` shows something you chose.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Clean up at a known point -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: `IDisposable` plus a `using` block runs `Dispose` deterministically the moment the block ends.
task.6.summaryClose: These are type-system essentials, not C# trivia - most object languages have an abstract type, an overridable method, a custom text form, and a cleanup hook. Next, you meet the collections and queries that store and shape many of these objects at once.
concept.pr-abstract-type.def: A base that describes a shape its subtypes must fill in and cannot itself be created with new.
concept.pr-override.def: Replacing a base type's virtual behaviour in a subtype, while code holding the base still calls the real object's version.
concept.pr-overloading.def: Giving two methods the same name but different parameters, so the compiler picks the right one from the arguments.
concept.pr-tostring-override.def: Overriding ToString so a type decides how it prints, instead of showing its type name.
concept.pr-idisposable.def: Implementing IDisposable so a using block runs Dispose at a known point, even if something inside fails.
